name: Hair gel

lead: Hair gel is a styling product that holds hair in a chosen shape. It is worked through damp or dry hair and dries into a firm or flexible hold, with finishes from wet-look to matte.
The appearance payoff is control: a cut keeps its shape, flyaways stay down, and styles such as slick-backs, quiffs and spikes become possible on hair that would not hold them alone.

paras: Gel is applied by hand and shaped with fingers or a comb. Products are often sold by hold strength, with higher numbers holding more firmly in North America and the UK, and some are formulated for Afro-textured hair. Results last until the hair is washed.

Allergic contact dermatitis from hair gel has been reported in a review of men's personal care products. A meta-analysis of frontal fibrosing alopecia and cosmetics examined hair gel among many products.

chain: Polymers bind to hair and stiffen as they dry
Style holds its shape through the day
angle.text: Gel lets a cut keep a defined shape, adding hold for spiked, slicked or textured styles. It is a temporary cosmetic effect that ends at the next wash.

lead: Hair gel is a hairstyling product used to harden hair into a particular style.[1] It is applied to the hair, dries to a hold, and lets users create shapes ranging from sleek and wet-look to spiked, giving a haircut definition that lasts through the day.

Hair is one of the most adjustable parts of appearance, and gel is among the simplest tools for it: a cut that would flop or frizz can be held in a quiff, slick-back or textured crop, and flyaways can be tamed. The effect is temporary and ends at the next wash.

Modern gel was developed in the 1960s in the US and is credited to the Dep brand, said to be named for its diethyl phthalate ingredient and its non-greasy feel; earlier fixatives included fat, pine resin and gum arabic.[1] Brylcreem was invented by Britain's Chemico Works in 1928 or 1929 and the fixative gomina by José Antonio Brancato in Buenos Aires in 1914.[1][2] Research on hair gel is mostly dermatological, concerning allergies and associations with scalp conditions.
infobox: Water base, film-forming polymers, thickeners, humectants [3]
Fat, pine resin, gum arabic, gomina, Brylcreem [1][2]
Numbered scales in North America and UK [1]

paras: Cationic polymers are among gel's main functional components, according to Wikipedia: their positive charges stretch and thicken the gel and bind it to negatively charged sites on hair keratin.[1] Reference text describes gels as water-based, with a film-forming polymer for hold, a thickener such as carbomer, humectants such as glycerin, and sometimes ethanol for faster drying, with higher polymer concentration giving firmer hold.[3] A physics study used hair gel and shaving foam as model yield-stress fluids, meaning materials that hold shape until enough stress makes them flow.[4]

Types include numbered hold-strength gels, formulas for Afro-textured hair, 'spiking' gels associated with 1980s hardcore punk, and gels with temporary colour.[1] Finishes range from shiny wet-look gels to matte formulas, and some products are alcohol-free or marketed as natural.[3]

Reference text describes working gel through damp or towel-dried hair for short styles, shaping with fingers for texture or a comb for a sleek finish, scrunching for curl definition, and letting the style set without touching it.[3] Hair is typically styled with a small amount, and styles last until the hair is washed; repeated use without washing is described as leading to build-up.[3]

Wikipedia reports that gel is used by people from Mediterranean regions, Eastern Europe, the Arab world and Latin America, as well as by people with African-descent hair textures, and ties particular gel styles to subcultures.[1]

Analysis of ancient Egyptian mummies by a team led by Natalie McCreesh found a fat-based gel in the hair of people from a Dakhleh Oasis cemetery, with the oldest about 3,500 years old.[1] The Irish bog body Clonycavan Man, dated to 392-201 BC, had a gel made of pine resin, probably imported from Spain or southwest France.[1]

In 1914 José Antonio Brancato created gomina in Buenos Aires, whose name became a generic term for fixative and displaced earlier soaps and oils.[1] Brylcreem, an emulsion of water and mineral oil stabilised with beeswax, was made in Birmingham by Chemico Works in 1928 and led the British and American styling market for decades; Unilever bought the global rights in January 2012.[1][2] Modern gel arrived in the 1960s.[1]
Reference text links later gel use to punk and rock spikes in the 1970s, slicked-back hip-hop styles in the 1990s, and a shift toward natural and alcohol-light gels in recent years.[3]

sections.h: Gel compared with pomade, wax and clay
paras: Wikipedia's pomade article says pomades are greasy, waxy or water-based, hold longer than most hair-care products and made the pompadour, ducktail and quiff possible; it describes pomades as most popular from the 1920s to 1950s, declining afterward and returning in the 2010s with the undercut.[5] It says firm-hold gels dry stiff and can usually only be restyled by wetting the hair, whereas oil-based pomade stays malleable, and water-based pomades wash out more easily than oil-based ones.[5]

The hair wax article says wax, often sold as pomade, putty, paste or molding gum, remains pliable and has less chance of drying out than gel, which mostly contains alcohol.[6] The quiff itself is described as a combination of the 1950s pompadour and flattop that returned in the early 1980s and 1990s.[7]

A review of allergic contact dermatitis from men's personal care products identified hair gel among implicated products and listed para-phenylenediamine, minoxidil, methylisothiazolinone, musk ambrette and cocamidopropyl betaine among the most common allergens across products.[8] A systematic review and meta-analysis examined the relationship between frontal fibrosing alopecia and personal care products including hair gel among many others.[9]

Reference text notes that ethanol-containing gels can dry hair, that fragrance is a leading cause of cosmetic contact dermatitis, and that diethyl phthalate and microplastics are subject to regulatory attention in some regions.[3] It also notes that product buildup can dull hair and may irritate the scalp.[3]
A 2024 forensic study evaluated hair fixatives including gels as microtraces transferred from hair to footwear.[10]
No studies found on gel's styling effect. Dermatology reviews have examined allergy and alopecia associations with personal care products.[8][9]

timeline.event: Fat-based gel is found in hair of ancient Egyptian mummies, the oldest about 3,500 years old.[1]
Clonycavan Man in Ireland wears pine-resin hair gel.[1]
Morgan's Pomade is founded in the UK.[5]
José Antonio Brancato creates gomina in Buenos Aires.[1]
Chemico Works in Birmingham makes the first Brylcreem.[2]
Modern hair gel is developed in the US.[1]
Spiking gels become associated with hardcore punk.[1]
Pomade and strong-hold products return with the undercut.[5]
Unilever buys global Brylcreem rights from Sara Lee.[2]
